source: Schroeder & Cenkci (2018) spatial contiguity meta-analysis (German summary sheet read) and Beege et al. (2019) Spatial continuity effect vs spatial contiguity failure
finding: The split-attention (extraneous load) effect is said to depend on material complexity. The meta-analysis gives a medium overall integration benefit. Beege et al. state that high-complexity material gave large effects and low-complexity material gave small non-significant ones, and they chose high-complexity material on purpose to replicate the effect. They attribute the d values to earlier work (Ginns 2006, Schroeder & Cenkci 2018), so the pair is second-hand.
numbers: Schroeder & Cenkci: g = 0.63 overall for integrated vs separated picture and text (worksheets g = 0.80, 2D pictures g = 0.71). Beege et al. quote d = 0.78 (high complexity) vs d = 0.28, p > .05 (low complexity). Beege et al. own experiments: N1 = 98, N2 = 85, high-complexity material only; medium distance beat near and far.
quote: When complexity is low, only small effect sizes (d = 0.28; p > 0.05) could be observed.
limits: The summary sheet does not list a complexity moderator. The 0.78 vs 0.28 pair could not be traced to a table. Beege et al. used only high-complexity material, so they do not test the interaction. A search found no preregistered independent test of the interaction.
agent_relevance: Human support for the interaction is between-study moderator evidence, not a clean within-study replication. It supports the S0 idea (aids matter when load is high) at weak strength.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters & Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect, Learning and Instruction 98:102142
finding: A search confirmed the meta-analysis exists and is in Learning and Instruction (not Educational Psychology Review). The effect sizes d = 0.505 (novices) and -0.428 (experts) in our earlier notes were not confirmed from the paper.
numbers: No pooled effect size could be verified this session.
limits: Only bibliographic hits were seen. Do not cite effect sizes until the paper is opened.
agent_relevance: Keep K05 single-source. The expertise-reversal analogue for the agent (gap 9) must be tested on our own tasks.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context length alone hurts LLM performance despite perfect retrieval
finding: Even when the model can recite the needed evidence perfectly, accuracy falls as the input gets longer. The fall remains when the filler is whitespace and when all filler tokens are masked from attention. A fix is to make the model recite the evidence first and then solve from a short prompt.
numbers: Drop of 13.9 to 85 percent across 5 models on math, QA and code as length grows to 30K tokens. Llama and Mistral lose at least 7 percent with whitespace filler, up to 48 percent (Llama, variable summation) and 30 percent (Mistral, GSM8K). Closed models drop less, mostly under 10 points, with larger single cells (one MMLU cell about -67.6; the row-to-model mapping is garbled in the extracted text). Recite-then-solve: Mistral-7B on GSM8K at 26,250 tokens 35.5 baseline vs 66.7 (up to +31.2 points); GPT-4o up to +4 points on RULER QA2.
limits: Models up to Mistral-7B, Llama-3, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5/3.7, Gemini 2.0; no 2026 frontier models. Length is not split by task load, so this does not test the CLT interaction.
agent_relevance: Context cost exists even with no distractors. A step that shortens context before reasoning (recite or summarize state) is a restructure that is not plain decomposition. It is a candidate for the S0/O3 area.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math lowers accuracy. Plain chain-of-thought and program prompts fall off on problems with four or more reasoning steps. Least-to-most decomposition stays flatter across step count. So the distractor cost grows with the number of steps, the same direction as the CLT interaction.
numbers: code-davinci-002, rows read from the main table: CoT micro 73.5 (2-step) vs 70.8 (more than 2 steps), overall 72.4, macro 6.0. Least-to-most micro 74.9 vs 81.5, overall 77.5, macro 18.0. With the instruction 'feel free to ignore irrelevant information' CoT reaches 77.8 micro, 15.0 macro. Text: text-davinci-003 macro accuracy is 0 on problems with more than 2 steps for role-overlap distractors.
limits: 2022-23 models. The table in the extracted text is partly misaligned, so only rows I could read with confidence are given. Micro and macro are different metrics (macro counts a base problem only if all variants are right).
agent_relevance: Gap 4: extra context hurts more on multi-step problems, not only on low-load ones. This matches the human interaction in direction (extraneous material costs more when load is high) and does not support the idea that context hurts only low-load items.

source: Dellibarda Varela et al. (2025) Rethinking the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Re-ran Hanoi and River Crossing with Gemini models. Stepwise prompting (ask for the next p moves from the current state, so each output is short) beat one-shot, but both stepwise and agentic-dialogue variants still fail around N = 8 disks. So output length explains part of the collapse, not all. In River Crossing, restricting to solvable instances lets models solve very large ones (over 100 agent pairs).
numbers: Hanoi N = 3 to 10, 10 trials per configuration. Agentic dialogue struggles from N = 4 and loops forward and backward without converging. Stepwise success drops clearly as N nears 8. Per-N rates are in figures, not in the text read. River Crossing: hardest solvable cases were (N = 4, k = 3) and (N = 5, k = 3); decomposed prompting did not clearly improve on the original study.
quote: previously reported failures solving the Towers of Hanoi were not purely result of output constraints, but also partly a result of cognition limitations
limits: Single model family (Gemini). Comparison to the original paper uses curves estimated by eye from published plots. Small trial counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: chunking the output removes the length excuse and the collapse stays near 8 disks, so part of the collapse is a state-maintenance limit, not only formatting.

source: Lawsen (2025) Comment on The Illusion of Thinking (v2, re-read)
finding: Asking for a program instead of a move list gave high accuracy on Hanoi with 15 disks across several models in under 5,000 tokens. The comment also says the River Crossing set includes unsolvable instances for N above 5 with boat capacity 3. Version 2 admits the first token-limit argument rested on a wrong reading and now uses 10 tokens per move.
numbers: Prompt: 'Solve Tower of Hanoi with 15 disks. Output a Lua function that prints the solution when called.' Models: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5. Result reported as 'very high accuracy'; no table; the author calls the experiments preliminary.
limits: No numbers or per-model rates, not peer reviewed. Only Hanoi was tested with the procedure format; no non-Hanoi task was run.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open outside Hanoi. Hanoi has a short known recursive rule, so a function is easy to write. A task with no compact procedure would not gain.

source: Pereira & Zuidema (2026) Transformers struggle to use their emergent world models: revisiting the Tower of Hanoi
finding: Standard tower-to-tower Hanoi is saturated for current reasoning models. The flat-to-flat variant (discs spread over pegs at start and goal, so the joint configuration must be tracked) is much harder. Probes show the models encode the board state at the end of the prompt and lose it while generating moves. Injecting the prompt-time state back repairs a large share of failures.
numbers: Standard: DeepSeek-R1 24/25, Kimi-K2-Think 23/25, gpt-oss-120b 25/25, Qwen3.6-27B 24/25 solved; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 1/25. Flat-to-flat: strongest models solve about half optimally; Qwen3.6-27B optimal 4/33 at n = 6 and 2/33 at n = 7 (32k output budget). Steering: weakest strength turns 52 percent of failures into optimal solutions; best setting lifts Qwen3.6-27B from 33 to 59 of 81 (41 to 73 percent).
limits: Unpublished master thesis, two open models, one puzzle family. Steering needs white-box access.
agent_relevance: Solution length is similar but interactivity differs: the standard puzzle rides on a memorised recursion, flat-to-flat needs the joint state. This supports counting joint-state load rather than solution length. Practical: restate the full state at each step (explicit state write-back).

source: Wolf, Rothberg, Shteyman & Shashua (2025) Compositional hardness of code in large language models, a probabilistic perspective
finding: Putting two sub-problems in one context makes success harder than solving them separately, beyond what the product of the two success rates predicts. The gap grows with solution length. The sub-problems are independent, so the penalty is not caused by dependency between steps; it is a cost of sharing one context.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 200 samples per problem, HumanEval and Code Contests pairs: composition needs up to 10 to 20 times more generations than the product of the parts. Llama-3-70B is better on pairs, but with four contest problems most compositions need 5 to 10 times more generations. Mistral-7B shows the same pattern (appendix).
limits: Coding only, 2024 open models. The composition is a concatenation of two separate problems, not a shared-variable (interacting) task. Theory assumes noise added to logits of the second problem.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a clean contrast with sub-answer content held fixed and context sharing changed. It shows part of the decomposition benefit is context separation, not only shorter chains. Arity inside one step is still not separated.

source: Schnabel, Tomlinson, Swaminathan & Neville (2026, v5) Lost in transmission: when and why LLMs fail to reason globally (BAPO)
finding: A formal measure of how much information must cross between token positions (bandwidth, BAPO) predicts which tasks fail, independent of input length. Low-bandwidth tasks stay accurate as n grows; high-bandwidth tasks (reachability, majority, variable tracking) fail on small instances. Chain of thought is proven to turn any hard task into easy steps; o3 and Gemini 2.5 Flash do well on hard tasks but with a very large number of reasoning tokens.
numbers: GPT-4o, Claude and Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash: high accuracy on BAPO-easy tasks across n; low or rapidly falling accuracy on BAPO-hard tasks at small n (binary tasks, chance 50 percent, 95 percent CI). Exact numbers are in figures.
limits: Pre-reasoning models in the main figures. The measure is task-class level, not item level, and not a rater-made element count.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a structure-based predictor can beat length on matched designs. It is a formal cousin of element interactivity (what must be combined at once) and computable without a rater for synthetic tasks.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with language models
finding: Decompose only when the executor fails (recursive, as needed) and compare with always-plan (plan-and-execute) and never-plan (ReAct). As-needed decomposition beat both on three text environments. The depth used rose with task depth.
numbers: GPT-3.5, test sets. ALFWorld success: ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6 (dmax 3). WebShop: ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, ADaPT 44.0. TextCraft: ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, ADaPT 52.0 (dmax 4). TextCraft by recipe depth: depth 2: ReAct 26.9 vs ADaPT 78.2; depth 3: 1.8 vs 38.7. Mean max depth used 1.9 at recipe depth 2, 2.8 at depth 3. Weak executor (atomic skills only) rose from 3.3 to 41.7 percent.
limits: The gate is a failure signal after execution, not an estimate of load before it. Tokens are not matched; ADaPT makes more calls. GPT-3.5 and 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: closest measured evidence that gated beats always-decompose and never-decompose. The gate is failure, not predicted load, so an S0 load gate is still untested. Depth grows with real difficulty, as CLT would predict.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. CoT gives large gains on symbolic, math and logic tasks and almost nothing elsewhere. On MMLU, CoT helps mainly when the question or answer contains an equals sign.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic reasoning +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9 points. Top-three-category average 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. All other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. About 32 percent (59) of the benefiting dataset-model pairs in the top categories were significant after Bonferroni (p < 0.00027).
limits: Prompted CoT on 2024 models. The authors say the small gain elsewhere is not a win because CoT costs more tokens. Does not test element counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: scaffold benefit concentrates in symbolic multi-step tasks (high interactivity); elsewhere it is cost without gain. Supports a gate that skips scaffolds on low-load items.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Tasks where verbal deliberation hurts people also hurt models with CoT. Over-scaffolding has a measured cost on implicit-pattern tasks.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning: GPT-4o direct 87.5 vs CoT 64.4 (-23.1); Claude 3 Opus -8.0; Gemini 1.5 Pro -6.05; Llama 3.1 70B -8.8; Claude 3.5 Sonnet +1.8 (not significant). o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o direct 94.0 on the subset (-36.3, a cross-model comparison). Face recognition (MCQ, chance 20 percent): GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8. Classification with exceptions: GPT-4o needed 2.9 vs 12.5 iterations to learn the labels (direct vs CoT).
limits: Three failure archetypes out of six tested; 2024 models. Not matched on tokens, so length and content effects are not separated.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: over-scaffolding can cost 20 to 36 points on tasks that do not need explicit steps. Rule for S0: do not scaffold perceptual or implicit-pattern tasks.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 technical report, prompting note
finding: The authors report that few-shot prompting consistently degrades R1 and recommend zero-shot with a stated output format. This is a model-level cousin of expertise reversal: a model trained to reason does worse with an added worked-example scaffold.
numbers: No table; one sentence in the discussion.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: One sentence, no numbers, one model family. Examples may hurt through format or length, not only through redundant guidance.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: scaffold depth and example-giving should depend on model class. Test few-shot on and off per model on our items.

source: Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) Beyond confidence: rethinking self-assessments for performance prediction in LLMs
finding: The model rates its own effort, ability and confidence. Self-rated effort and ability predict its failures at least as well as confidence, and effort is best on reasoning-heavy tasks. A self-estimated load-like quantity (effort) carries signal about the model's own errors.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 38 tasks, 8 domains. Best single dimension beats confidence by 10.1 and 8.4 AUROC points (proprietary, open) on standard tasks and 6.7 and 8.9 points on hard tasks. On a task subset: GPT ability AUROC 0.89 (confidence via multi-step 0.88, top-k 0.89); Claude ability 0.89; Qwen effort 0.89; Llama effort 0.83.
limits: Predicts correctness of the same model on the same item, not objective difficulty. I did not check in each prompt whether the rating came before the answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a cheap self-rating of effort is plausible as an S0 signal, but it must be asked before answering and checked on our own items.

source: Li et al. (2026) Can LLMs estimate student struggles? Human-AI difficulty alignment with proficiency simulation for item difficulty prediction
finding: Over 20 models, zero-shot difficulty estimates match human item difficulty only weakly, and larger or reasoning models do not do better. Difficulty ratings also do not predict the model's own errors well.
numbers: Spearman rho averages below 0.50; SAT Math about 0.41, USMLE about 0.13; GPT-5 0.34 vs GPT-4.1 0.44. Self-error AUROC hovers near 0.5 for most models (table rows show a few higher cells, e.g. GPT-4.1 0.73 on Cambridge and 0.72 on SAT-R). Predictions cluster narrowly and skew easy.
limits: Target is human difficulty, not the model's own difficulty. Educational items, not reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a direct 'how hard is this' rating is a weak signal. It contrasts with d14 where effort and ability ratings work. Elicitation form matters: ask about own effort, not difficulty for others.

source: Kolesnikova et al. (2026) Estimating item difficulty with LLMs as experts; Acquaye et al. (2026) Take out your calculators: LLM student simulations
finding: LLMs as raters of item difficulty give moderate to strong rank correlation with empirical difficulty on primary-school maths. Pairwise comparison beats absolute rating unless token probabilities and known-difficulty examples are added. Simulating students and fitting item response theory beats direct judgement.
numbers: Kolesnikova: Spearman by domain, full factorial of format x decision type x prompt style, three models; human experts in earlier work vary and some are below .50 (Bejar 1983). Acquaye: correlations up to 0.75, 0.76 and 0.82 for grades 4, 8 and 12 against NAEP; direct LLM judgement is poor.
limits: Human item difficulty on school maths. Per-domain numbers for Kolesnikova are in tables I did not extract. Acquaye abstract and first page only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a rater-made score gets decent rank correlation with human difficulty, and human experts are noisy too. No work found that compares a rater element count with length on LLM failure.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Let's learn step by step: in-context curriculum learning (ICCL)
finding: Ordering demonstrations from simple to complex improves in-context learning for instruction-tuned open models but not base models.
numbers: Average +9 percent F1 vs random order and +7.8 percent vs VoteK on the reported tasks; base models lack sensitivity (one decline of 7.16 percent).
limits: Orders demonstrations, not reasoning steps; NLP classification-style tasks; 2024 open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 (indirect): sequencing helps modestly and only for instruction-tuned models. It is not a test of isolated elements first inside one problem.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Problem-solving logic guided curriculum in-context learning for LLMs complex reasoning
finding: Choosing demonstrations by problem-solving logic and ordering them by step count from easy to hard beats prior selection methods on average. In the ablation, ordering alone adds little.
numbers: Llama3-8B on SVAMP, AQuA, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA: average with order 70.79 vs without order 70.55 for the authors' selection (+0.24); other strategies differ by about 0.5 (random selection 71.70 vs 71.17). Some table rows are misaligned in the extracted text.
limits: One 8B model, few-shot demonstrations only, tiny differences, no significance tests seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: ordering by step count is worth about half a point or less here, so sequencing may not be the main lever. Whether load can be changed beyond decomposition stays open for agents.

source: Kang, Zhao, Hsu & Lee (2024) On the empirical complexity of reasoning and planning in LLMs
finding: Case studies on 6 tasks link CoT and tree-of-thought gains to decomposition into low-sample-complexity steps. At the same token budget, ToT is only marginally better than CoT on GSM8K and worse than CoT self-consistency there, while it clearly wins on Game of 24.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; per-task numbers were not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and intro were read in detail; the matched-token statement is from the introduction text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: under matched tokens, structured search pays off on computationally hard tasks and is roughly neutral on easy ones. This is the shape a load gate should exploit.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad, re-read for the distractor curve and ID50 table
finding: The U-shaped distractor curve is in the data (quadratic term significant for most models) but is strongest at middle difficulty and short length, and the frontier models are almost flat. The paper gives no mechanism. The generator may confound the curve: at fixed N, a low needle ratio means very few relevant updates (a short effective chain), and hay statements are built to change only non-target people. That is my reading of the generation rules, not a result in the paper.
numbers: At d = 1 the curve is nearly flat; at d = 5 the dip is widest (needle ratio 25 to 50 percent); at d = 10 mean accuracy gpt-5 0.821, o3 0.804, gpt-5-mini 0.675, o4-mini 0.646, gemini-2.5-pro 0.654, DS-R1-0528 0.475. Trough fades as N grows: clear at N = 20, nearly flat for the strongest models at N = 100, mostly flat by N = 250. gpt-5 0.97 / 0.89 / 0.91 and o3 0.93 / 0.89 / 0.88 across low / mid / high ratio. Five models have non-significant ratio terms. ID50 where the table was legible: DS-R1-0528 19.07, gpt-5-mini 14.78, gemini-2.5-pro 12.74, DS-Llama-70B 10.86, gemini-2.5-flash 8.56, QwQ-32B 4.08, Qwen3-8B 1.0, Qwen3-32B -0.55, Phi-4-mini-reasoning -3.95. Several frontier cells are misaligned in the extracted table and were not used.
limits: Nothing re-run. The mechanism note is hypothesis only. ID50 mixes entities and attributes, so it is not the same as k interacting elements.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly answered: the U-shape fades for the strongest current models and long N, and grows with intrinsic difficulty (as the human interaction predicts). Gap 3: ID50 spans below 0 to about 19, so the best k differs by model and must be measured per model.
